title: Sensor- and Simulator-Based 3D Visualization of Acupuncture Points – A Pilot Study
summary:
The number of physicians with a specialty certification in acupuncture in Germany has grown from 2,113 in 2005 to 15,602 in 2024. Precise point localization is a central precondition for the effectiveness and comparability of acupuncture treatments.  This exploratory pilot study primarily aims to validate the use of a simulator ("Virtual Man"), originally designed for teaching acupuncture points, as a measurement tool for analyzing them.
The aim is to establish a foundation for standardizing the localization of acupuncture points and acupuncture techniques. The “Virtual Man” acupuncture training system will be used, which is designed to enable precise measurement of needle position both on the body’s surface and within the tissue.
The position of the acupuncture needles will primarily be determined using two methods: 1. Electromagnetic tracking via the system itself and 2. Using a 3D sensor-based measurement method.
Secondarily, the variance in needle positions will be examined. For this purpose, up to 80 physicians certified in acupuncture, with at least 200 hours of certified continuing education and at least two years of clinical acupuncture experience will be invited to participate.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
The study includes specialists with additional qualifications in acupuncture who have at least two years of clinical experience using acupuncture and who continue to perform acupuncture treatments regularly. Additionally, they must have given written consent to participate in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
The simulator uses a low-energy electromagnetic field for three-dimensional positioning of the needles (electromagnetic tracking, EMT). The magnetic field strength of the electromagnetic position transmitter is ≤ 200 µT. This field is considerably below the safety limits relevant for humans. These fields are harmless to healthy individuals. A field strength of approximately 200 µT is well below the threshold that could potentially affect implantable medical devices (e.g., pacemakers, ICDs, neurostimulators), and no noticeable interference is generally expected. During operation, the transmitter is located under a silicone human model. The distance between a user with, for example, a pacemaker and the transmitter source should generally not be less thanbe at least 60 cm, which is considered safe. However, as a precautionary measure, it is recommended that users with pacemakers should avoid leaning directly over the central area of the device during usethe procedure. A moderate distance does not affect use. All participants are explicitly informed of the existing risk in advance in the information sheet and are advised of this it before the intervention begins.
